prize_parts.citation: for the theoretical prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and Z2 topological insulators and its first experimental observation in HgTe quantum wells

statement.case_for: After reading the full first round I keep B008 as a single coherent achievement. Kane and Mele introduced a classification principle (the Z2 invariant for time-reversal-invariant insulators) that did not exist before, and Molenkamp's group confirmed the predicted helical edge transport in HgTe quantum wells within about two years, with the quantised conductance and non-local signatures reproduced by others. Fifteen to twenty years of independent confirmation, including photoemission in many materials, make the interpretation stable. This is the one shortlisted case where a general concept, a specific material prediction and a quantitative experiment line up with three names, and it is neither early nor late. I looked again at whether the clock could displace it as my first choice. It has moved up, because Kroll showed that the magic-wavelength condition is a genuine concept and not just engineering, but I still judge the conceptual content and the open scientific consequences of the Z2 principle to be larger.
statement.case_against: The main weakness is the 2016 prize for topological phase transitions and phases of matter. I argue that time-reversal-invariant topological insulators and quantum spin Hall edge states are a separate principle, but a committee may see the topological idea as already honoured. Attribution is also not clean. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang proposed HgTe as the platform, Fu, Kane and Mele and Moore and Balents are entangled for three dimensions, and Hasan's photoemission work sits outside my trio. Any three-name cut leaves out real contributors, and I cannot claim to have settled this. If the committee judges that the 2016 prize leaves too little room, my honest fallback is B043, which has the cleanest attribution on the list.

responses.point: Pearce, as chair, supports a two-part prize of optical lattice clocks (Katori, Ye) plus IceCube credited to Halzen alone, and asks whether a one-name IceCube credit is defensible.
responses.response: I do not think a one-name IceCube credit is defensible, and that is the reason I would not support this configuration. A lone name for a detector built and operated by hundreds, with Karle and Yoshida having real claims, would be contested as soon as it was announced. His own text concedes that the decisive work was collective. Dropping the IceCube half and keeping B043 alone is better than pairing it with an arbitrary credit. I also notice that the two-part design is driven by the three-person cap and not by the science, since Pearce and Danielsson themselves doubt that B043 stands alone. Pairing unrelated fields dilutes both, and I would rather the committee choose one coherent achievement.

responses.point: Kroll argued that the magic-wavelength condition is a concept that removes the trade-off between trapping atoms and perturbing the clock transition, which the 2005 comb prize did not address.
responses.response: This changed my view in part. I had called the clock a technical refinement, and I now accept that the magic-wavelength lattice is a concept with a verified payoff and that it is distinct from counting optical cycles in 2005 and trapping single ions in 2012. That is why B043 is my first alternative and not merely a courtesy listing. It still seems to me that the prize would honour a change in what can be measured rather than a principle about how matter behaves, since no deviation from existing theory has been seen and the redefinition of the second has not happened. He concedes as much. We differ on how much that distinction should count, not on the facts.

responses.point: Olsson ranks twisted bilayer graphene first, accepts that topological insulators are mature and well confirmed, and identifies the fourth name (Hasan, Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang, Fu, Moore) as the weak point of any three-person cut.
responses.response: I agree that the attribution is the weak point of B008, and I do not think it can be fully resolved. The credit that fits the claim is the quantum spin Hall effect, not the three-dimensional story, and that is why I keep Mele with Kane and Molenkamp. The Z2 classification is the principle, and Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang is the proposal that guided the experiment. A citation limited to the prediction of the effect and the HgTe observation is accurate even if it omits Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang and the 3D work. On B029 I understand her argument that the platform and phenomenology are reproduced by many groups, and I have moved a little. My remaining objection is that the pairing mechanism is open and Cao, Fatemi and Dean cannot be fitted into the cap. I still put maturity and attribution above novelty, and I would keep B029 as an alternative rather than first.

responses.point: Lindroth defends the clock as a clean two-name achievement that tightens bounds on varying constants and is more than a tool, and notes that attribution in fluctuation theorems is too diffuse for confident three names.
responses.response: She is right about fluctuation theorems. In round 1 I lowered B032 for the same reason, and I do not propose it now: the Evans-Cohen-Morriss lineage and the four credited names mean the committee could not name three with confidence. I also accept her point that the clock has delivered measurable bounds and not only promises. Her question about what a clock teaches that earlier prizes did not remains my main hesitation, but Kroll's answer on the magic wavelength narrows the gap. The remaining difference between us is whether the Z2 principle teaches something more fundamental than the ability to measure at 1e-18, and I think it does.

responses.point: Eriksson keeps twisted bilayer graphene as first choice with a citation limited to flat bands and observed correlated states, and has stepped back from DMFT.
responses.response: I respect the step back from DMFT, since my objection was that it is a method whose approximation is weakest in low dimensions. On B029 his proposal to name the flat-band prediction and the correlated insulating and superconducting states, without the mechanism, answers part of my maturity objection, because those statements are established. It does not answer the attribution problem, where Cao and Fatemi did the 2018 experiments and the Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto precursor sits beside Bistritzer and MacDonald. I therefore keep B029 as an alternative and would not oppose it, but I would not put it above B008 this year.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards the 2016 topological prize as leaving room for the Z2 and quantum spin Hall principle; this is the single most important open question for B008.
Whether leaving out Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, who proposed HgTe as the platform, would be judged unfair, and whether Mele or Hasan is the better third name beside Kane and Molenkamp.
Whether the clock's lack of any deviation from existing theory, and the pending redefinition of the second, should count against B043 as a scientific discovery or only as a delay in an application.
Whether the twisted bilayer graphene pairing mechanism will be settled soon enough to change my judgement of B029's maturity; this is a judgement about physics I cannot make with certainty.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict apparent. None of the credited names for B008, B043 or B029 appears among my documented connections, and my own work (stochastic processes, turbulence, neural networks) does not overlap with these candidates. I have no new disclosure since round 1.
